title: The third day
hookLine: the resurrection is the hinge of Christian faith (1 Corinthians 15:14)

cards: A church is starting to wobble. Some of its members have begun saying there's no such thing as rising from the dead. Maybe Jesus's resurrection is just a lovely way of talking.

A letter writer could soften it: even without it, the teaching is still beautiful, the example still inspiring. Paul, writing to that church in Corinth, does the opposite. He puts everything on the table.
In effect, he says: if this didn't happen, the whole thing falls. Every sermon, every prayer, every hope. He calls it vain.
Empty. Today's word is the line in the creed that everything hangs on. After he descended, the creed says: the third day he rose again from the dead.

teach.b: In First Corinthians 15, Paul says he's passing on what he himself received, a short summary he didn't make up: "that Christ died for our sins according to the scriptures; And that he was buried, and that he rose again the third day according to the scriptures."

teach.h: FIVE HUNDRED AT ONCE: GO ASK THEM.
teach.b: Then he lists who saw him: Peter, the twelve, more than five hundred people at once, most of them still alive, Paul adds, as if to say, go and ask them. James. And last of all, Paul himself.

teach.h: THE HINGE: IF NOT, IT'S VAIN.
teach.b: Then the hinge: "And if Christ be not risen, then is our preaching vain, and your faith is also vain." The New Testament doesn't tell it as a nice metaphor for spring, or for the teaching living on.
The Gospels tell of an empty tomb found by women at dawn, and a risen Jesus who can be touched, who eats fish, who still carries his wounds, and yet is changed, sometimes not recognized at first.
The Apostles' and Nicene Creeds both confess it. Some modern Christian thinkers have read it more spiritually; the creeds speak of a rising from the dead, and the conversation goes on.
The Greek word is anastasis, standing up again.

teach.h: HE ROSE AGAIN THE THIRD DAY.
teach.b: All through the Easter season, Orthodox Christians greet each other with three words, Christ is risen, and the answer, He is risen indeed. Death is not the end: that's the claim the whole faith hangs on.

how: Christians celebrate the resurrection at Easter, and Sunday, the day the Gospels name for the empty tomb, is kept as a little Easter; Orthodox Christians greet each other with "Christ is risen" through the Easter season.

games.q: you're Paul. some in the Corinthian church say there's no resurrection of the dead. what do you write?
o: it doesn't really matter; the teaching is still beautiful.
if Christ is not risen, our preaching and your faith are vain.
let each believe what they like.
games.why: Paul puts everything on it: "And if Christ be not risen, then is our preaching vain, and your faith is also vain."

practice: Picture the garden in the dark before dawn, from the Easter chapters, Mark 16 or John 20: the stone, the women walking with spices, what they expected to find, and what they found instead.

In John, Mary Magdalene meets the gardener, and he says her name. If you pray, pray the old Easter greeting, Christ is risen; if you don't, stay with the women in the garden, in that moment of surprise.

wordCard.voice: Anastasis. The Greek word for resurrection, standing up again: Christ risen on the third day, and everything hanging on it.

orig.note: Greek: standing up again, resurrection. Also the name of the Orthodox Easter icon.

carryVoice: Your line: death is not the end. Christ is risen; he is risen indeed. That's day three hundred four.
